title: The Calling of Nyami Nyami
subtitle: The Great River God of the Kariba Gorge
illustrationCaption: Tonga elders and children gathered at twilight as the sacred serpent glides under the moonlit Zambezi.
moral: When humanity honors and protects the rivers that give them life, nature rewards them with peace, abundance, and safe passage.
paragraphs: Long before concrete walls rose across the mighty gorges, the Zambezi River flowed free and untamed, carving its path like a silver serpent through the heart of southern Africa. The BaTonga people, who lived along its sun-drenched valley, knew that this water was not merely an ordinary river; it was the living home of Nyami Nyami, the great River Spirit.

Nyami Nyami was an awe-inspiring guardian. Elders described him with the head of a regal fish and the glistening body of a dragon serpent, his emerald and ochre scales catching the golden brilliance of dawn. Whenever he swam beneath the surface, gentle green waves lapped against the riverbanks, filling the fishing baskets with bream and blessing the sorghum fields with sweet morning dew.

In those days, no Tonga fisherman pushed his wooden dug-out canoe into the current without whispering a song of thanks to the sacred waters. 'Twabomba, Mukwai,' they would chant softly, dipping their palm into the cooling stream. And in return, Nyami Nyami protected them from fierce hippos, hidden sandbanks, and turbulent white-water rapids.

One season, severe drought scorched the plateau above the valley. While inland streams dried into cracked mud, the Zambezi continued to flow full and pure. A young fisherman named Mainza set out with his little sister Lweendo to carry water to the parched villages in the hills. As their canoe drifted into the Kariba Gorge, a sudden mysterious whirlpool swirled beneath their paddle.

Neither child panicked. Remembering the elder Mweene's teachings, Mainza lowered his head and offered a handful of roasted maize into the swirling pool. Slowly, the water settled into calm glass. From the emerald depths, a majestic serpentine silhouette crested above the surface, its amber eye shining with benevolent warmth.

Nyami Nyami acknowledged their humble respect with a low, rumbling call that resonated through the rocky canyon walls like distant summer thunder. With a graceful flick of his caudal fin, he directed a gentle current that carried their canoe smoothly to the landing shore, where fresh springs bubbled up through the rocks to nourish their people for generations to come.

vocabulary.definition: The revered river god and protector of the Zambezi Valley in BaTonga traditional folklore.
The indigenous Bantu ethnic group indigenous to the Middle Zambezi Valley in southern Zambia and northern Zimbabwe.
The tail fin of a fish or sea creature used for powerful forward propulsion.
A traditional respectful greeting and expression of heartfelt gratitude.

questions.question: What physical form did the elders use to describe Nyami Nyami?
options: A winged lion with golden claws
The head of a fish and the body of a serpent
A giant crocodile with elephant tusks
A silver fish with human hands
questions.explanation: Tonga folklore describes Nyami Nyami with the head of a fish and the long serpentine body of a water dragon.

questions.question: How did Mainza and Lweendo show respect when the whirlpool appeared?
options: They threw stones into the water
They offered roasted maize with humility
They jumped out and swam away
questions.explanation: Following ancestral wisdom, Mainza offered roasted maize and bowed his head in humble respect.

questions.question: What is the central moral lesson of the story?
options: Living in harmony and showing respect to nature brings protection and abundance
Maize grows best by the riverside
questions.explanation: The story teaches that reverence, gratitude, and care for natural waters reward humanity with safety and peace.

title: Mosi-oa-Tunya: The Smoke That Thunders
subtitle: The Sacred Rainbow and the Children of the Leya
illustrationCaption: Two young Leya explorers gaze in awe at the thundering cascades and vibrant double rainbow of Mosi-oa-Tunya.
moral: True courage is not fearless arrogance, but listening with open ears and quiet awe to the timeless majesty of the natural world.
paragraphs: Miles before one reaches the edge of the great chasm, the earth vibrates with a deep, rhythmic bass note. White towers of vapor rise hundreds of meters into the sky like great billowing clouds of mist. To travelers from distant lands, this spectacle is called Victoria Falls; but to the Leya people who have safeguarded its basalt cliffs for centuries, its true name is Mosi-oa-Tunya—'The Smoke That Thunders.'

In the ancient royal village of Mukuni, high above the gorge, young Mwamba and his cousin Natasha were learning the sacred stories of their ancestors. Their grandfather, Chief Mukuni, sat beside the council fire with a polished fly-whisk carved from leadwood. 'The gorge,' the elder whispered, 'is where the sky touches the river in an eternal dance. Where the spray rises, ancestral spirits weave rainbows of hope.'

On a crisp morning at the start of the dry season, the cousins were entrusted with gathering aromatic lemongrass along the edge of the rainforest trail that fringed the falls. As they walked beneath the dense emerald canopy of ferns and wild fig trees, fine droplets coated their skin like cool morning silk.

Suddenly, through a parted veil of mist, they stepped upon the knife-edge cliff. Before them stretched an endless precipice of falling water. Millions of liters plunged over basalt columns, crashing into the churning boiling pot far below. Arcing across the canyon was a brilliant double rainbow, glowing with emerald, gold, indigo, and fiery crimson.

Mwamba gasped, instinctively stepping back from the sheer drop. Natasha gently took his hand. 'Do not fear, Mwamba,' she smiled softly. 'Listen to the sound. It is not anger; it is the heartbeat of our land.'

Closing their eyes, the children stood in reverent silence. Beneath the roar, they heard the sweet trill of trumpeter hornbills and the gentle whisper of river wind. When they opened their eyes, they felt not fear, but profound pride: they were the children of Mosi-oa-Tunya, guardians of the earth's most spectacular wonder.

vocabulary.definition: The indigenous Toka-Leya name for Victoria Falls, translating literally to 'The Smoke That Thunders.'
A dense, dark volcanic rock formed from cooling lava that makes up the dramatic gorges of Victoria Falls.
A very steep or overhanging mass of rock; a sheer cliff face.
The deep, swirling whirlpool canyon located directly below the Victoria Falls bridge.

questions.question: What does the indigenous name 'Mosi-oa-Tunya' mean?
questions.explanation: 'Mosi-oa-Tunya' is the ancient Toka-Leya name meaning 'The Smoke That Thunders'.

questions.question: What natural feature arched across the gorge before the children?
questions.explanation: A radiant double rainbow arced through the spray and mist across the basalt canyon.

questions.question: What helped Mwamba overcome his fear on the cliff?
options: He ran away to the village
His cousin reminded him to listen to the falls as the heartbeat of the land
He threw a pebble down the cliff
questions.explanation: Natasha reminded him that the thunder was the land's heartbeat, bringing reverent peace rather than fear.

title: The Water Maidens of Musonda Falls
subtitle: The Enchanted Cascades of the Luapula Valley
illustrationCaption: A gentle village girl carrying water lilies watches luminous firefly water spirits dancing over stepped granite tiers.
moral: Kindness offered without expectation of reward illuminates even the darkest shadows and brings harmony to the community.
paragraphs: In northern Zambia, where the crystal Luapula River winds through rolling green hills, Musonda Falls tumbles over stepped granite shelves like a staircase of foamy lace. The local Aushi and Chishinga elders speak of magical water spirits—the *Bana-Chola*—who watch over the cascading pools, ensuring the fish spawn in peace and the wild water lilies never wither.

In a nearby village lived an orphan girl named Bupe. While others spent their afternoons playing games by the banana groves, Bupe would walk down to the lowest pool of Musonda Falls carrying her clay pot. She never used harsh tools or broke the reeds; instead, she gently weeded fallen branches from the stream and placed fragrant white lilies along the rock edges.

One warm twilight, as the sun dipped behind the miombo woodlands, Bupe noticed a trapped Kingfisher struggling in an abandoned fishing net near the churning spray. Without hesitation, she stepped carefully over the slippery stones, untangled the bird's turquoise feathers, and watched joyfully as it darted safely into the sky.

As she turned back toward the bank, the waterfalls began to glow with a soft, ethereal luminescence. Hundreds of golden fireflies rose from the mist, clustering into delicate dancing silhouettes that hovered over the crystal pools. They were the legendary Water Maidens of Musonda.

A voice as melodious as bubbling brook-water echoed in Bupe's heart: 'Little daughter of the earth, you who protect the winged creatures and respect the cool waters, your heart is pure as granite springwater.' The spirits gently touched her clay pot, leaving a circlet of luminous river pearls around its rim.

From that day onward, whenever Bupe dipped her pot into Musonda Falls, the water remained clear, cool, and sweet for weeks, bringing health and healing to the elderly and sick of her village. Bupe never bragged about her gift, knowing that the purest treasures are those given out of gentle love.

vocabulary.definition: A widespread southern African woodland ecosystem characterized by distinctive Brachystegia trees.
Extremely delicate, light, and heavenly in a way that seems not of this world.
Light emitted by a substance not resulting from heat, such as the gentle glow of fireflies.
A traditional Zambian name meaning 'Gift'.

questions.question: What animal did Bupe rescue from the fishing net?
questions.explanation: Bupe carefully untangled a trapped kingfisher with turquoise feathers from an abandoned net.

questions.question: What gift did the Water Maidens bestow upon Bupe's clay pot?
options: A circlet of luminous river pearls
questions.explanation: The spirits touched her pot, leaving a ring of luminous river pearls that kept the water sweet and healing.

questions.question: Why did the Water Maidens choose to bless Bupe?
options: Because she brought them gold coins
Because she was the fastest runner in the village
Because she treated the river, reeds, and animals with selfless kindness
Because she sang the loudest songs
questions.explanation: The spirits rewarded Bupe's humble and consistent care for the river and its living creatures.

title: Makumba: The Sacred Sky Stone
subtitle: The Heavenly Messenger of the Luapula Plateau
illustrationCaption: Elders and youth gather with reverent wonder around Makumba, the sacred meteorite stone beneath an ancient fig tree.
moral: True wisdom seeks to understand the mysterious forces of the universe rather than attempting to conquer or exploit them.
paragraphs: Centuries ago, in the highlands of Luapula near Chief Chishinga's ancestral court, the night sky was torn open by a blinding arc of cyan fire. A star seemed to fall from the heavens, accompanied by a sound like twenty drums beating in unison. When dawn broke, the villagers found a smooth, dark metallic stone resting peacefully beneath an ancient wild fig tree.

The stone was unlike anything found in the surrounding red earth. It possessed a faint celestial sheen, cool to the touch even in the scorching midday sun, yet humming with a faint, musical vibration when tapped with a copper bangle. The elders named it *Makumba*, meaning 'The Visitor from the Sky.'

Soon, rumors of the extraordinary meteorite reached a greedy warlord in a neighboring valley. Believing the stone possessed magical power to forge invincible spears, he marched with forty warriors to haul Makumba away. But no matter how many ropes they tied around the stone, and no matter how many men strained their backs, Makumba refused to budge even a finger's breadth.

Frustrated, the warlord struck the stone with a heavy iron mallet. Instantly, a flash of white light leaped from Makumba, harmlessly disarming every warrior and melting the tips of their iron weapons into smooth, harmless beads. Trembling in awe, the warriors fled back through the forest.

That evening, an elder herbalist named Nakulu approached Makumba with quiet respect. She brought no ropes, no weapons, and no demands—only a small gourd of freshly ground millet meal and a cup of pure stream water. She laid them before the stone and bowed her head in thanks for the blessing of peace.

To this day, the Chishinga people regard Makumba as a sacred emblem of cosmic balance. It reminds every traveler that heaven's gifts are meant to unite humanity in quiet wonder, never to be stolen for war or selfish gain.

vocabulary.definition: A solid piece of debris from an asteroid or comet that survives its passage through the atmosphere to reach the ground.
A celebrated sacred stone meteorite venerated in Luapula oral history as an ancestral celestial messenger.
Belonging to or relating to heaven or the deep starry skies.
A respectful Bemba/Aushi term of endearment for a grandmother or elder matriarch.

questions.question: What happened when the greedy warlord tried to strike Makumba with an iron mallet?
options: A flash of light disarmed the warriors and melted their weapons
The stone rolled away into the river
questions.explanation: Makumba emitted a brilliant flash of light that disarmed the warriors and safely melted their weapon tips.

questions.question: What did the wise elder Nakulu offer to the stone?
options: Ground millet meal and pure stream water
questions.explanation: Nakulu approached with peace, offering humble millet meal and stream water in gratitude.

questions.question: What is the lesson of the Makumba stone?
options: Nature and cosmic gifts are meant for peace, not selfish greed or war
questions.explanation: The story teaches that heaven's gifts must be treated with reverent wonder, not used for violence or exploitation.

title: The Moon Leopard of Lake Bangweulu
subtitle: The Silent Guardian of the Papyrus Lagoons
illustrationCaption: A luminous golden-eyed leopard perches gracefully upon a fallen log amidst misty papyrus reeds and blooming water lilies.
moral: Patience and quiet observation reveal truth that haste and loud words will always overlook.
paragraphs: Where the open waters of Lake Bangweulu give way to endless emerald swamps of swaying papyrus, the boundary between land, water, and sky melts into a dreamlike mist. Fishermen who navigate the labyrinth of channels speak of *Ngohe*, the Moon Leopard—a magnificent feline with a coat spotted like dappled starlight and eyes that glow like burning amber.

Unlike savanna leopards that hunt beneath the dry acacia branches, the Moon Leopard was said to glide silently across floating reed-mats and fallen water-logs without making a single ripple. It was not a predator of fear, but a watchful guardian that protected the breeding lagoons of the black lechwe antelopes and the nesting grounds of the rare Shoebill stork.

A young reed-cutter named Kalenga had worked for three seasons trying to find his way to the fabled 'Lagoon of Seven Lilies'—where the sweetest water-chestnuts grew. Driven by haste, Kalenga paddled vigorously every evening, chopping at reeds and shouting to scare away marsh-frogs, but each time he found himself lost in confusing cul-de-sacs of black water.

One night, as the full moon climbed into a cloudless velvet sky, Kalenga's canoe drifted against a moss-covered log. Exhausted and frustrated, he laid down his paddle and simply listened. The marsh fell silent. Soon, the rhythmic clicking of night crickets filled the air, accompanied by the gentle sigh of the breeze through the papyrus stems.

Looking up, Kalenga gasped in awe. Standing atop the curved log, bathed in silvery moonlight, was Ngohe. The Moon Leopard looked directly into Kalenga's eyes with tranquil calm. It did not roar or bare its teeth; it simply turned its graceful head and stepped gently along the bank, pausing at every bend to glance back.

Kalenga dipped his paddle silently, following the moonlit trail the leopard carved through the fog. Within moments, the dense reeds parted, revealing the shimmering surface of the Lagoon of Seven Lilies. Kalenga realized that nature's greatest sanctuaries are never discovered by brute force, but through quiet patience and attentive wonder.

vocabulary.definition: A vast lake and wetland system in northern Zambia whose indigenous name means 'Where the Water Meets the Sky.'
A tall aquatic sedge plant with feathery flower heads that grows extensively in African freshwater swamps.
A graceful, long-hoofed water antelope indigenous to the marshes and floodplains of southern-central Africa.
A complex, maze-like network of intersecting pathways or water channels.

questions.question: What is unique about the Moon Leopard's behavior in the Bangweulu swamps?
options: It hunts fish with iron claws
It glides gracefully across logs and protects the wildlife without violence
It swims underwater like a crocodile
questions.explanation: The Moon Leopard moves silently over floating mats and logs, acting as a serene guardian of the wetlands.

questions.question: Why did Kalenga repeatedly get lost during his earlier searches?
options: He rushed impatiently and made loud noise instead of observing quietly
questions.explanation: Kalenga acted with haste and loud commotion, which blinded him to the natural flow of the channels.

questions.question: What lesson did Kalenga learn when he reached the Lagoon of Seven Lilies?
options: Patience and quiet observation reveal secrets that haste misses
Water lilies only grow under moonlight
Papyrus reeds should be cut down
questions.explanation: The story emphasizes that patience, silence, and reverent observation reveal life's greatest treasures.

title: The Mukuni Fire Walkers and the Sacred Flame
subtitle: The Legend of the Timeless Campfire at Batoka
illustrationCaption: Wise elder Mukuni holding his carved serpent staff beside the sacred fire, recounting oral histories to attentive youth under a starry sky.
moral: Knowledge passed from elders to the young is a living flame; when nurtured with respect, it never extinguishes.
paragraphs: Perched atop the ancient plateau overlooking the roaring gorge of Livingstone lies Mukuni Village, one of the oldest continuously inhabited royal settlements in southern Africa. In the central *insaka*—the village gathering circle—a small log fire has been kept burning for hundreds of years. The Toka-Leya people call it *Mulilo wa Kale*, the Fire of Remembrance.

According to oral tradition, this sacred fire was originally kindled from a lightning strike that touched a towering mopane tree during the great drought of antiquity. Ever since, each generation of elders has tended the coals with aromatic wild olive wood, ensuring the village never loses its warmth, its counsel, or its memory.

Each new moon, the youth of Mukuni gather in a wide semi-circle around the coals. On this evening, an elder named Bwana Sikute leaned upon his carved serpent staff. His silver hair caught the flickering amber light as he spoke to the attentive children: 'A tribe without its stories is like a tree whose roots have forgotten the soil. It may look green for a season, but the first storm will topple it.'
A young boy named Chanda asked, 'Grandfather, why do we not simply use matches to light a new fire whenever we need one? Why carry the coals through rain and wind?'

Sikute smiled warmly and placed a dry twig onto the glowing heart of the fire. Within seconds, a joyful golden flame leaped upward, showering the night with fragrant cedar sparks. 'Because, Chanda, this fire did not begin with us, and it will not end with us. Every spark you see contains the laughter of your grandmothers, the courage of your grandfathers, and the prayers of ancestors who walked these cliffs before kings had names.'

Chanda bowed his head, feeling the warmth spread across his hands and heart. He understood then that the fire was not just burning wood; it was the sacred, unbroken chain of culture, belonging, and community that bonded all their people into one.

vocabulary.definition: A traditional Zambian open-air village pavilion or round shelter where community meetings, meals, and storytelling take place.
The indigenous people inhabiting the southern Zambezi borderlands around Victoria Falls and Livingstone.
A resilient hardwood tree prevalent in southern African river valleys, prized for durable wood and fragrant aroma.
Tonga/Leya phrase meaning 'The Ancient Fire' or 'The Eternal Fire of Ancestral Memory.'

questions.question: What is the name of the traditional village storytelling circle?
questions.explanation: An 'insaka' is the traditional open-air pavilion and community circle used for elder storytelling.

questions.question: What did the elder Sikute say a tribe without its stories resembles?
options: A tree whose roots have forgotten the soil
questions.explanation: Sikute taught that without oral heritage, people are like trees with forgotten roots that fall in storms.

questions.question: What does the eternal campfire symbolize to the villagers of Mukuni?
options: A way to keep wild animals away
An unbroken chain of heritage, ancestral memory, and community love
A method for cooking daily food only
questions.explanation: The fire symbolizes the living, unbroken continuum of ancestral wisdom and shared communal identity.

title: The Secret Cavern of Batoka Gorge
subtitle: The Lost Rock Paintings of the Ancient Hunters
illustrationCaption: Two brave children carrying a brass lantern marvel at ancient red-ochre rock art inside an emerald underground pool cavern.
moral: True heritage is our shared responsibility to discover, honor, and protect for those who come after us.
paragraphs: Far downstream from Victoria Falls, the Zambezi River cuts through the zigzagging canyons of the Batoka Gorge. Here, sheer basalt walls rise hundreds of meters above turbulent Class V rapids. In these shadow-cloaked cliffs lie hidden caverns known only to cliff-nesting falcons and wandering goat herders.

During school holidays, two adventurous cousins, Mapalo and Kunda, were helping their uncle search for a stray calf along the high rim of the third gorge. Following faint hoofprints down a steep goat track, Mapalo slipped slightly, catching himself against a cleft in the rock face. Behind a curtain of wild jasmine vines, they noticed a cool breeze drifting from an arched opening in the stone.

Mapalo lit an old brass kerosene lantern he carried in his satchel. Holding the yellow flame aloft, the cousins stepped cautiously into the cavern. The roaring sound of the river outside immediately faded into a reverent, cavernous hush.

Before them opened a breathtaking subterranean chamber. At their feet lay a pool of crystalline turquoise water so calm it resembled polished glass. But what made both children gasp was the cavern wall: stretching across the limestone was a magnificent gallery of ancient rock art painted in rich red ochre, charcoal, and white clay.

There were leaping elands with curved horns, running hunters carrying light bows, swimming hippos, and at the center, a gigantic arched river serpent crowned with fish fins. 'Look,' whispered Kunda with wide, glistening eyes. 'The ancestors were here thousands of years ago. They painted our river spirit before paper or books existed!'

Mapalo and Kunda sat by the lantern light, tracing the centuries-old outlines with their eyes without touching the fragile pigment. When they emerged into the afternoon sunshine, they did not reveal the cavern to treasure hunters; instead, they reported their discovery to the Livingstone Museum curators, ensuring the ancient sanctuary would be preserved with the dignity and protection it deserved.

vocabulary.definition: The dramatic, narrow 120-kilometer canyon carved by the Zambezi River downstream from Victoria Falls.
A natural clay earth pigment containing ferric oxide, used for millennia by indigenous African artists for rock paintings.
Existing, occurring, or situated beneath the surface of the earth.
A place of safety, refuge, or sacred preservation.

questions.question: What did Mapalo and Kunda discover behind the curtain of wild jasmine vines?
options: A hidden chest of gold coins
An ancient cavern with rock art and a turquoise pool
questions.explanation: They found a concealed limestone cavern containing ancient rock paintings and an underground pool.

questions.question: What images were painted on the cavern walls?
options: Elands, hunters, hippos, and an arched river serpent
questions.explanation: The walls featured ancient ochre paintings of elands, hunters, hippos, and the sacred river serpent.

questions.question: What responsible action did the children take after leaving the cave?
options: They informed the Livingstone Museum curators to safeguard the site
They carved their own names on the cave paintings
They sealed the cave entrance with rocks
questions.explanation: The children protected heritage by reporting the discovery to museum curators for preservation.

title: The Singing Baobab of Luangwa
subtitle: The Tree of Life in the Valley of the Elephants
region: South Luangwa National Park & Eastern Province
illustrationCaption: Two Zambian children sit beneath the colossal branches of an ancient baobab in the golden Luangwa savanna as birds sing.
moral: When we protect the oldest living beings on our earth, they reward us with shelter, wisdom, and life-giving shade.
paragraphs: In the wide floodplain of the South Luangwa Valley, where leopards nap in sausage trees and herds of elephants march along sandy riverbeds, stands an ancient baobab tree so enormous that twelve grown men holding hands cannot encircle its girth. The local Kunda villagers call it *Muti wa Nyimbo*—'The Singing Tree.'

This baobab is not ordinary wood and bark. It has stood for more than a thousand years, weathering droughts, bushfires, and torrential seasonal floods. In its massive hollow trunk, bees build hives of wild amber honey, lilac-breasted rollers nest in its hollows, and weary travelers find dry shelter from sudden storms.

Villagers say that whenever the dry season wind blows across the savanna at sunset, the hollow knots in the baobab's branches whistle with gentle melodic harmonies, as if the tree itself is singing ancient lullabies to the grazing impalas and giraffes.

One sweltering afternoon, young Tembo and his little sister Thandi were walking home when an unseasonal dust storm blew across the plains. Swirling red dust blinded their vision and howled through the dry grass. Remembering their mother's instructions, Tembo held Thandi's hand tightly and led her into the arched wooden hollow of the singing baobab.

Inside, the air was surprisingly cool, peaceful, and scented with dried cream-of-tartar fruit. High above them, the tree trunk groaned softly with deep soothing tones, filtering the ferocious wind into gentle music. Outside, the storm raged, but inside the ancient giant, the children felt as safe as if they were wrapped in their grandmother's Chitenge blanket.

When the storm passed and the sun set in a glorious explosion of amber and violet, the children stepped out onto the refreshed savanna. As they looked up into the leafy canopy teeming with chattering birds, Tembo touched the smooth grey bark. 'Thank you, grandfather tree,' he whispered. In the golden glow, both children knew they would spend their lives protecting the wild wonders of their Zambian homeland.

vocabulary.definition: A colossal African deciduous tree with an exceptionally thick trunk, able to store thousands of liters of water and live for thousands of years.
A renowned national park in eastern Zambia celebrated globally for abundant wildlife and pristine savanna ecosystems.
An iconic southern African bird recognized by its breathtaking rainbow plumage of green, turquoise, and violet.
A vibrant, ornately patterned 100% cotton wax-print fabric worn across Zambia for ceremonies and daily life.

questions.question: What is the special name the villagers gave to the ancient baobab tree?
questions.explanation: The villagers call it 'Muti wa Nyimbo', which translates to 'The Singing Tree'.

questions.question: How did the baobab tree protect Tembo and Thandi?
options: It sheltered them safely inside its hollow trunk during a violent dust storm
It bent its branches into stairs
It created a water puddle for them
questions.explanation: The hollow trunk provided cool, safe sanctuary from the ferocious dust storm.

questions.question: What resolution did the children make as they left the baobab at sunset?
options: To chop down the tree for firewood
To dedicate their lives to protecting the wild wonders and natural heritage of Zambia
To build a house in its branches
To hunt the animals in the valley
questions.explanation: Filled with gratitude, the children pledged to protect Zambia's ancient trees and wild natural wonders.
